summary: Looks at the benefits and problems of allowing RTCP packets to be smaller by relaxing the compound packet rules in RFC 3550. Based on that analysis, it defines certain changes to those rules for sessions that agree to use them.

plainLanguage.summary: Status reports in a call usually come in big bundles. This note lets some reports be sent as small slips instead, which saves space when the bundle is not needed.

questions: can rtcp packets be sent without compound packets
when can rtcp skip the compound packet rules
does reduced-size rtcp work with srtp
subtitle: Lets feedback messages in an RTP session travel as small RTCP packets instead of always riding in a full compound packet.

tldr.problem: RTCP packets must be sent as compound packets with a sender or receiver report plus a CNAME item, which makes even the smallest packet large. On slow or lossy links, urgent feedback arrives late or gets lost.
tldr.mechanism: For sessions using the AVPF or SAVPF profile in Early RTCP or Immediate Feedback mode, the RFC lets extra feedback be sent as Reduced-Size RTCP, while regular reports stay compound. Support is signalled with the SDP attribute a=rtcp-rsize.
tldr.outcome: Feedback such as NACK or codec control requests can be sent cheaply and quickly. The catch is that old receivers and middle boxes may discard the smaller packets, so senders must verify delivery. The RFC updates RFC 3550, RFC 3711 and RFC 4585.

today: RFC 5506 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3550, RFC 3711 and RFC 4585, so it is the place that defines Reduced-Size RTCP and the a=rtcp-rsize attribute.

sections.title: Why Compound Packets Are a Problem
sections.content:
In RTP, RFC 3550 makes it mandatory to send RTCP as compound packets: a sender report (SR) or receiver report (RR), followed by a source description (SDES) packet that carries at least the CNAME item. That makes even the smallest RTCP packet quite large.

The RTP/AVPF profile (RFC 4585) adds feedback messages that benefit from being sent with minimal delay. On low-bitrate links these messages can still use many resources and take extra time to send as part of a compound packet. This RFC therefore proposes sending just the feedback, as Reduced-Size RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every little note has to be sent inside a big envelope, even if the note is tiny. On a slow road, the big envelope arrives late.

sections.title: What Compound Packets Are For
sections.content:
Before relaxing the rule, the RFC lists why compound packets exist. Sender and receiver reports tell every participant which SSRCs are in the session, so everyone can estimate the group size, which the RTCP transmission scheduling relies on. Failing to do so could make RTCP senders use too much bandwidth. The reports also give basic statistics for monitoring and adaptation.

The CNAME item lets receivers decide which media flows should be synchronized, and sender reports carry the NTP and RTP timestamps used to do it. The CNAME is also the longer identifier used to tell an SSRC collision from an RTP-level routing loop.

The RFC concludes that both the SR/RR and the CNAME are very important, especially for new participants, and that their value drops if they are not sent regularly.
sections.plainLanguage: The big envelope holds a head count, a name tag and a clock check. Newcomers need those, so the envelope still has to be sent regularly.

sections.title: Use Cases and Benefits
sections.content:
The RFC names four use cases: control plane signalling (the Open Mobile Alliance Push-to-talk over Cellular service), codec control such as TMMBR messages from RFC 5104, feedback such as generic NACK for video, and small status reports that could even be sent unencrypted for network monitoring.

The size saving is concrete. An RR with a report block for one source is 32 bytes and an SR is 52 bytes. The SDES packet with a CNAME is 10 bytes plus the CNAME string length. A Reduced-Size RTCP packet can therefore be at least 70-80 bytes smaller than a compound packet.

Smaller packets are less likely to be dropped on links where loss grows with packet size, such as radio links, and they take less time to serialize. The RFC gives the example that 120 bytes over a 30 kbps link takes 32 milliseconds. Smaller feedback also keeps RTCP bandwidth lower during heavy feedback periods.
sections.plainLanguage: A short note is less likely to get lost on a bumpy road and gets through the gate faster than a thick bundle.

sections.title: Known Issues
sections.content:
Section 3.4 of the RFC lists the problems. Middle boxes may drop RTCP that does not follow the compound rules, or treat an unfamiliar packet type as unknown, so compound packets might get through while Reduced-Size ones are lost.

Packet validation code in RFC 3550 Appendix A would discard Reduced-Size RTCP. Updated validation is weaker, since it can no longer insist that the first packet is an SR or RR. Old receivers would drop the small packets entirely, which can split a session into old receivers that see only compound feedback and new ones that see both. It can also skew the avg_rtcp_size calculation.

SRTP (RFC 3711) says the first part of an SRTCP packet must be an SR or RR, but the RFC finds SRTP has no real dependency on that, so Reduced-Size RTCP can be used with it, though SRTP implementations MAY need changes. Multiplexing RTP and RTCP on one port and header compression raise further points that are left partly to future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old mail sorters throw away anything that is not a big envelope. So you have to check that your small slips really arrive.

sections.title: When Reduced-Size RTCP Is Allowed
sections.content:
The RFC says regular compound RTCP MUST keep being sent throughout the session, so group size tracking and synchronization still work and newcomers can learn about the senders. Reduced-Size RTCP SHOULD be limited to extra RTCP, such as feedback, sent when a regular compound packet would not otherwise have been sent.

It SHALL only be used in sessions running AVPF (RFC 4585) or SAVPF (RFC 5124) in Early RTCP or Immediate Feedback mode, and SHALL NOT be sent until at least one compound RTCP has been sent. In Immediate Feedback mode all feedback MAY be Reduced-Size. In Early RTCP mode, feedback scheduled as Early RTCP MAY be, but anything scheduled as Regular RTCP SHALL be compound.

A Reduced-Size RTCP packet holds one or more RTCP packets of any type, MUST NOT be used for regular scheduled reports, and MUST NOT be used with the RTP/AVP or RTP/SAVP profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Small slips are only for urgent notes. The big bundle must still go out on schedule, and you can only use slips after you have sent at least one bundle.

sections.title: Verifying Delivery
sections.content:
Because packets may be dropped by old endpoints or middle boxes, applications MUST use an algorithm to detect consistent failure to deliver Reduced-Size RTCP. The details are application dependent and outside the scope of the RFC.

Where delivery can be detected, it is easy to check. A sender report is confirmed by the echoed timestamp in a later receiver report. Many feedback messages show up as an effect, such as an RTP retransmission (RFC 4588) after a NACK, or a TMMBN after a TMMBR. Packet types whose delivery cannot be detected SHOULD NOT be sent as Reduced-Size RTCP unless they share a datagram with a type that can be.

If verification fails, it is strongly RECOMMENDED to fall back to compound RTCP only. For size-sensitive links, sending a single RTCP packet per lower-layer datagram is strongly RECOMMENDED, and large Reduced-Size packets should just be sent as compound ones.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send a small slip, look for a sign that it arrived, like a reply. If no signs come, go back to using the big envelope.

sections.title: Signalling With SDP
sections.content:
The RFC defines the a=rtcp-rsize SDP attribute to show that a participant can support Reduced-Size RTCP. A participant that proposes its use must itself support receiving it. An offerer wanting it MUST include the attribute in the offer, and an answerer that supports and wants it SHALL include it in the answer.

In declarative uses of SDP, such as RTSP or the Session Announcement Protocol, the attribute means the participant MAY use Reduced-Size RTCP. IANA registered rtcp-rsize as a media-level property attribute that takes no value.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides say "I can read small slips" before anyone sends one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RTP and AVPF also apply. The weaker validation of received packets on the RTCP port may lead to spurious data being accepted as real RTCP. This can mostly be addressed by any security mechanism that provides authentication, for example SRTP (RFC 3711).
sections.plainLanguage: With looser checking at the door, fake slips could sneak in. A secret handshake, such as SRTP, keeps them out.
